Since points are finite, every allocation forecloses another, and the tree's shape communicates that cost visually before the player commits. Good trees make trade-offs legible and let a specialisation feel like a plan; weak ones present an illusion of choice, where most paths converge or a single branch is obviously superior to the rest.

Blizzard North's Diablo in 1996 gave each class a page of skills tied to levels, in a game built around repeated runs whose reason to start again is to build differently. Visual layout mattered as much as the mathematics, since a chart shows a possible future in a way a list of numbers cannot. Its sequel expanded this into the large synergy trees that most later implementations imitate.

Trees spread far beyond role-playing games because they attach a visible plan to any progression, which keeps players oriented across long sessions. Same ubiquity is the complaint: many trees are filler, offering percentage increases that change nothing about play, and a respec button quietly removes the opportunity cost that justified the structure. Designers now argue for smaller trees with fewer, sharper decisions instead.
f_skill_tree.spread: Deus Ex spent points on non-combat capability, Borderlands made trees the difference between characters, and Horizon Zero Dawn used them to teach its systems gradually.
f_skill_tree.question: Which game invented the skill tree?

f_loot_rarity.lede: Colour-coded loot rarity assigns each item a colour that signals its tier at a glance, turning evaluation into an instant read rather than a comparison of statistics.
body: Item generation picks a rarity tier, then rolls properties within that tier's range, and the display colours the item's name accordingly. White is ordinary, blue better, gold or orange exceptional. Player learns the language in minutes and can then triage a floor of drops without opening anything. Colour also drives feeling directly, since the flash of an unusual tint is a reward delivered before its contents are known.

Blizzard North needed players to sort through enormous quantities of generated items in Diablo in 1996 without stopping to read, because the game's loop is killing and looting at speed. Colour is the cheapest possible interface for that, requiring no text, no icon and no localisation. Convention it established proved so effective that games in unrelated genres adopted the same palette without ever explaining it.

One-glance value became the medium's most portable interface convention and, in parallel, its most exploitable. Rarity colours make a randomised drop feel like an event, which is exactly the property loot boxes and gacha systems monetise, and the flash works whether the item beneath it matters or not. Designers who want players to read items rather than colours now have to work against the expectation.
f_loot_rarity.spread: World of Warcraft attached tiers to raiding, Borderlands escalated the palette into orange and beyond, and Destiny 2 tied it to seasonal power caps.
f_loot_rarity.question: Why are rare items in games colour-coded?

f_gear_score.lede: A numeric gear power treadmill reduces equipment to one ascending number, letting a game gate content by that figure and replace every item on a schedule set by its release calendar.
body: Each item carries a rating derived from its statistics, and a character's total becomes a single figure used for comparison, matchmaking and entry requirements. Number does two jobs: it tells a player whether an upgrade is really an upgrade, and it tells the game whether they are permitted into an activity. Simplification is deliberate, because comparing multi-statistic items across dozens of slots is work most players will not do.

World of Warcraft made the pattern explicit from 2004 onward, since a subscription game needs a reason to log in next month and raid tiers supply one only if last month's rewards stop being sufficient. Blizzard Entertainment tied progress to a treadmill that could be extended indefinitely with each patch. Everything a player earns is therefore scheduled for obsolescence before it is even awarded.

Treadmills make content plannable for a studio and legible for a player, which is why live-service games adopted them wholesale. They also devalue effort by design, generate gatekeeping in matchmaking, and reduce interesting build decisions to a single scalar. Alternatives exist, including horizontal progression where new gear differs rather than exceeds, but they are much harder to sell as an obvious reason to keep playing.
f_gear_score.spread: Destiny turned the figure into a weekly cap, Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn syncs it downward for old content, and Destiny 2 used it to structure seasons.
f_gear_score.question: What is gear score in online games?

f_perk_loadout.lede: Perk-based loadouts let players assemble their own class from unlocked weapons and modifiers before a match, replacing fixed roles with a personal configuration carried between games.
body: Player fills slots, typically a primary weapon, a secondary, equipment and two or three perks that alter movement, detection or damage. Choices persist across matches and are unlocked through play, so the loadout screen doubles as a progression display. Balance moves from designing roles to constraining combinations, since the interesting failures are rarely single overpowered perks but pairs that remove an entire counterplay option.

Infinity Ward's Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare in 2007 attached persistent unlocks to a competitive shooter that had previously handed everyone the same tools. Motivation was retention, because a match ending with a new attachment gives a reason to start another one. Design also flattered variety, since a lobby of players carrying different configurations produces a messier and more surprising match than symmetrical loadouts do.

Customisation became standard almost immediately, and with it the expectation that a competitive shooter is also a progression game. Costs are borne by newcomers, who face opponents holding tools they cannot yet earn, and by balance teams managing a combinatorial space. Games that resist it, keeping every player identically equipped, now market that decision as fairness, which shows how thoroughly the default has shifted.
f_perk_loadout.spread: Call of Duty: Black Ops added a currency for buying unlocks, Titanfall attached loadouts to pilots and mechs, and Dead by Daylight built asymmetric perks for both sides.
f_perk_loadout.question: Which game introduced custom loadouts and perks to shooters?

f_prestige.lede: Prestige lets a player who has reached the maximum rank reset all their progress in exchange for a symbol, converting completed progression into visible status and a fresh climb.
body: On hitting the level cap, a player is offered a reset that removes unlocks and returns them to the beginning, awarding an emblem and usually an extra loadout slot. Nothing is gained mechanically; what is gained is legibility to other players, since the badge appears beside a name. Choice is voluntary and public, which is the entire design, because the cost is real and everyone can see it was paid.

Infinity Ward added it to Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare in 2007 to solve a problem finite progression creates, which is that a player who has unlocked everything has no scheduled reason to return. Rather than extending the ladder, the design let players restart it. Trading power for a symbol works only because a multiplayer community is an audience, and status is worth something in front of one.

Prestige demonstrated that a progression system's real product is often display rather than capability, an idea now taken for granted across live-service games. Its descendants include seasonal resets, ranked ladders that wipe, and battle passes that expire. Critics see an infinite treadmill dressed as an achievement, and the mechanism does keep people playing for rewards that do nothing, which is either honest or cynical depending on presentation.
f_prestige.spread: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 added prestige-only unlocks, and Call of Duty: Black Ops let players spend each reset on permanent cosmetic tokens.
f_prestige.question: Why do shooters let you reset your rank for a badge?

f_meta_progression.lede: Run-persistent meta-progression lets a failed run leave something permanent behind, so a roguelike's deletion of the character no longer deletes the player's sense of forward movement.
body: Currency earned during a run survives death and is spent between runs on permanent upgrades, unlocks or new options in the generation pool. Each attempt therefore has two outcomes, the run itself and the deposit it makes. Tuning is delicate: too much persistence turns a skill game into a grind where failure is merely slow progress, too little and the structure offers nothing traditional permadeath did not.

Cellar Door Games released Rogue Legacy in 2013, framing persistence as an inherited family line where each dead hero's gold buys castle upgrades for a descendant. Fiction did a lot of work by making loss narratively appropriate rather than a concession. Timing mattered too, since a broad audience was discovering roguelikes through digital storefronts and finding the traditional form's total erasure hard to accept.

Compromise created the roguelite and with it one of the most commercially reliable structures in independent games, because it converts failure into a progress bar without removing risk. Purists argue that it undermines the point, since a player can eventually buy their way past a challenge they never learned to beat. Best implementations answer that by making persistence widen options rather than raise numbers.
f_meta_progression.spread: Dead Cells unlocked new weapons into the pool, Hades used spending as narrative, and Slay the Spire kept persistence deliberately thin to protect the integrity of its runs.
f_meta_progression.question: What is meta progression in roguelites?

f_soulslike_loop.lede: Bonfire checkpoints restore supplies and respawn every enemy when used, while death drops the player's accumulated currency where they fell and grants exactly one attempt to retrieve it.
body: Resting at a checkpoint refills healing charges and resets all ordinary enemies, so recovery and renewed difficulty arrive together. Dying leaves the player's currency, which is both experience and money, on the ground at the place of death; reaching it restores everything, while dying again on the way erases it permanently. Every decision to press forward is a wager with a visible stake and a known route back.

FromSoftware's Dark Souls in 2011 expressed difficulty through save design rather than through damage numbers, extending a structure the studio had used in its previous game. Placement of checkpoints became the actual level design problem, since the distance between a bonfire and a boss defines the cost of each attempt. Shortcuts looping back to a checkpoint are the reward for exploration, more than new areas are.

Loop demonstrated that tension can be manufactured entirely from persistence rules, and it made a specific rhythm of loss and recovery into a genre marker. Its costs are what players argue about: repeated walks back are tedious, respawning enemies punish curiosity, and the system asks for time as much as skill. Later games in the lineage have steadily shortened the walk while keeping the wager intact.
f_soulslike_loop.spread: Bloodborne pushed aggression into the recovery, Hollow Knight attached a ghost that must be defeated to reclaim currency, and Elden Ring softened the walk with dense checkpoints.
f_soulslike_loop.question: How does the bonfire and souls-loss system in Dark Souls work?

f_attract_premise.lede: Attract-mode premise uses short non-interactive vignettes between rounds to establish character and situation, the first fiction to reach arcade players with no gameplay attached to it.
body: Vignettes play automatically between stages, or while a cabinet waits for a coin. Nothing is controllable; characters simply act out a relationship, usually in a few seconds and using the same sprites the game already contains. Cost is close to zero and the payoff is characterisation, since a pursuer that is briefly pursued becomes a personality rather than a hazard. Attract sequences also demonstrated play to passers-by.

Namco's Pac-Man in 1980 inserted brief cartoons between mazes, in which a ghost chases and is then chased. Reason was partly commercial and partly humane, because a game with no ending needs punctuation, and a cabinet in a room full of competitors has to be watchable when nobody is playing. Character was also a deliberate strategy, aimed at an audience beyond the young men who played shooters.

Consequence was that fiction entered arcade games through the gaps rather than through the play, establishing a division of labour the medium has never fully resolved. Story arrived as something shown between the interactive parts, which is the direct ancestor of the cutscene and of every argument about cutscenes. Merchandising followed at once, since a character with a personality can leave the cabinet entirely.
f_attract_premise.spread: Dragon's Lair turned the vignette into the entire game, Karateka used the technique to set up a rescue plot, and Mortal Kombat used it to introduce a roster.
f_attract_premise.question: Why does Pac-Man have little cartoons between levels?

f_cutscene.lede: An in-engine cutscene takes control away and uses the game's own graphics to stage a scene, so story and play share one set of characters, one world and one visual language.
body: Engine drives characters through scripted actions while input is ignored or reduced, then hands control back. Because the same assets are used, a scene can cut to a location the player will later occupy, or show an antagonist doing something elsewhere. Length and frequency are the design levers, and the crucial question is always what a scene does that the playable portion could not have done instead.

Jordan Mechner's Karateka in 1984 cut between the approaching hero and events inside the fortress, including a princess and a captor the player had not yet met. Technique came from cinema literacy applied to an 8-bit computer, and it worked because rotoscoped animation was expressive enough to carry a moment without text. Nothing extra had to be stored, since the scenes reused the game's own sprites and backgrounds.

Scenes became the default way games deliver plot, and the argument about them started almost immediately, since taking the controller is the one thing an interactive medium is uniquely able not to do. Costs are concrete too, because cutscenes consume budget, resist localisation and interrupt pacing. Every later technique, from full-motion video to fully playable dialogue, is a response to the same unsolved tension.
f_cutscene.spread: Final Fantasy VI staged an opera with its own sprites, Metal Gear Solid built a directing language around them, and Half-Life refused to cut away at all.
f_cutscene.question: Which game had the first in-engine cutscene?

f_qte.lede: A quick-time event asks for a specific input at a specific moment during an otherwise non-interactive sequence, reducing participation to timing while the spectacle plays out as authored.
body: Prompt appears, a short window opens, and the correct button either continues the sequence or triggers a failure branch. Player has no positional control and no strategy, only recognition and reaction. Design value is that any authored animation, however complex, can be made participatory at almost no cost, which is why the technique attaches to scenes that would be impossible to build as real gameplay.

Dragon's Lair, produced by Advanced Microcomputer Systems in 1983, ran hand-drawn animation from a laserdisc, a medium that could play film but could not render anything. Only possible interaction was choosing which pre-filmed segment played next, so the game became a series of timed inputs against gorgeous footage. Term itself came later, from Shenmue, but the structure was fixed in the arcade in 1983.

Cheapness explains its persistence, since a studio can make a cinematic moment interactive by adding a prompt rather than a system. Same cheapness explains the contempt, because the input rarely expresses anything about the player beyond attention, and failure repeats a scene already watched. Modern use is mostly narrow, either as a deliberate gesture in interactive drama or as punctuation inside a real combat system.
f_qte.spread: Shenmue named the technique and used it for street incidents, God of War attached it to boss finishers, and Resident Evil 4 in 2005 hid it inside cutscenes.
f_qte.question: What is a quick-time event and which game started it?

f_branching_dialogue.lede: Branching dialogue trees present conversation as a set of chosen replies, each one opening or closing later options, turning talk into something the player navigates rather than watches.
body: A dialogue tree is a graph. Each node holds a line of NPC speech and a list of player responses; picking one moves you to another node, and some nodes set flags that alter what is available later or elsewhere. Early implementations used typed keywords rather than menus, so the branching was hidden inside a vocabulary the player had to assemble from rumours, letters and overheard names.

Origin Systems built the technique into Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar in 1985 because the game needed to test the player's ethics, and a test demands questions with answers. Conversation was the only interface capable of asking. Attribution is genuinely contested: text adventures had accepted typed input for years, and other role-playing games of the period experimented with keyword talk, so Ultima IV is best read as the point where dialogue became a designed structure rather than a parser trick.

Consequences run in two directions. Writing became combinatorial, so cost grew with every branch, and studios learned to fake width with options that quietly converge inside a single scene. Set against that, dialogue trees gave the medium a way to make players responsible for what their character says, which is the precondition for reputation systems, companion relationships and endings that actually differ. Critics have argued ever since that picking from a list is not the same as speaking.
f_branching_dialogue.spread: Fallout attached skill checks to individual lines, Planescape: Torment ran to novel length, Disco Elysium made the tree the entire game, and Undertale rewarded refusing to fight.
f_branching_dialogue.question: Which game invented branching dialogue trees?

f_morality_axis.lede: An explicit morality axis scores the player's behaviour on a visible ethical scale, then uses that number to unlock powers, change how characters react, and decide which ending appears.
body: Behaviour gets measured. Actions carry stated or hidden weights, a counter moves toward one pole or another, and thresholds gate abilities, prices, dialogue and endings. Implementations vary enormously in granularity: some track several named virtues independently, others collapse everything onto one good-and-evil slider with two colour-coded buttons per conversation. Nearly all of them expose the score somewhere in the interface, which changes how people play the moment they notice it.

Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar shipped in 1985 with an unusual problem to solve. Origin Systems wanted a role-playing game with no villain, in which the goal was to become a moral exemplar, and tracking eight virtues was the only way to make that goal checkable by a computer. Richard Garriott has described the design as a reply to criticism of his earlier games, where players were free to rob and murder townspeople at no cost.

Scoring ethics makes them tractable and shallow at the same time. Once players learn that generosity pays, the axis stops measuring morality and starts measuring optimisation, which is why so many games funnel people into playing consistently saintly or consistently monstrous rather than inconsistently human. Designers have spent decades trying to escape that trap, mostly by replacing the single axis with faction standing, or by refusing to show the number at all.
f_morality_axis.spread: Fallout tied the score to reputation, Knights of the Old Republic colour-coded powers by alignment, inFAMOUS gated whole skill trees, and Undertale judged players for optimising it.
f_morality_axis.question: Which game first gave the player a good versus evil score?

f_fmv.lede: Full-motion video builds a game out of filmed actors stored on optical media, with the player choosing which pre-recorded footage plays next rather than controlling a rendered character.
body: Footage is shot on a set with a cast and crew, compressed, and stored as clips that branch. Player input usually amounts to selecting a camera, a room or a moment of intervention, and the engine's job is to reach the next clip without a visible seam. Because every possible outcome must be filmed in advance, the design space is fixed on the shooting day and cannot be revised in code afterwards.

Digital Pictures released Night Trap in 1992, once CD-ROM drives gave home machines enough storage to hold video at all. Its material had been shot years earlier for a cartridge system that never shipped, which is part of why the credit is contested: laserdisc arcade cabinets had been playing branching filmed and animated sequences since the early 1980s, and several CD-ROM titles were in production simultaneously. What 1992 added was a mass-market console format.

Commercially the genre collapsed within about five years, killed by grainy compression, thin interaction and the arrival of convincing real-time 3D. Its residue is permanent, though: production values became a competitive axis, studios started hiring casting directors and composers, and the expectation that a game contains cinema outlived the technique that introduced it. Video also survived as a framing device, used for briefings, archive footage and deliberately artificial texture.
f_fmv.spread: The 7th Guest built puzzles around filmed ghosts, Command & Conquer used it for mission briefings, and Alan Wake 2 revived the technique decades later as deliberate texture.
f_fmv.question: Which game popularised full-motion video?

f_env_storytelling.lede: Environmental storytelling places narrative information in the arrangement of a space itself, so that players learn what happened by reading rooms, bodies and debris instead of watching a scene.
body: Nothing pauses. A barricaded door, a chalk message, a corpse holding a keycard next to an empty medical cabinet: each detail is an authored fact placed where movement will find it, and the player assembles a sequence of events from the residue. Good examples are legible without explanation and reward a second look; weak examples degenerate into scattered props that gesture at meaning without encoding anything a careful reader could reconstruct.

Looking Glass Technologies used the approach heavily in System Shock in 1994, partly out of necessity. Its station was a first-person space with no party members to talk to and no budget for cinematics, so the level itself had to carry the plot. Attribution is loose here, since adventure games and even early dungeon crawlers had staged meaningful scenery before; System Shock's claim rests on doing it systematically, across an entire connected location, as the primary narrative channel.

Making space the narrator lets a game tell stories without taking control away, which suits designs built around exploration and dread. Costs follow. Players who move quickly miss most of it, ambiguity is easy to mistake for depth, and by the 2010s critics were describing whole games as walking tours through the aftermath of more interesting events. Whether that critique lands depends on how much the arrangement rewards attention.
f_env_storytelling.spread: BioShock hid an ideology in its ruins, Dark Souls left history in level geometry, and What Remains of Edith Finch built each room as a biography.
f_env_storytelling.question: Which game pioneered environmental storytelling?

f_audio_log.lede: The found audio log is a recorded message left by an absent character, picked up as an item and played while the player keeps moving, delivering exposition without stopping the game.
body: Recordings are placed as collectibles. Each holds a monologue, often part of a numbered series scattered across a location, and playback continues over ordinary movement and combat so the fiction advances while control stays with the player. Most implementations add a menu where logs can be replayed, which matters because dialogue heard during a firefight is dialogue half missed. Voices belong to people who are usually dead by the time you hear them.

System Shock introduced the device in 1994 as a direct consequence of its setting. Looking Glass Technologies had a research station full of corpses, a protagonist who wakes up alone, and no cutscene budget, so email logs from the dead crew became the only way to stage a cast that could not appear. Recording audio was also far cheaper than animating characters, which made the technique attractive long after the technical constraint had lifted.

Few narrative devices have been imitated this literally. Audio logs solved the problem of story in a first-person game so cleanly that they became a default, then a joke: an entire species of character who narrates their own doom into a recorder for no plausible reason. Defenders point out that the format survives because it works, letting writers control pace and mood while the player is free to keep playing.
f_audio_log.spread: BioShock scattered them as period recordings, Dead Space used them for escalating panic, Gone Home turned them into diary narration, and Outer Wilds made them archaeology.
f_audio_log.question: Which game invented the audio log?

f_voice_acting.lede: Full voice performance means every line of dialogue in a game is recorded by an actor rather than displayed as text, making performance part of the writing itself.
body: Recording everything changes the production pipeline more than the game. Scripts must be locked before studio time, actors are directed line by line without seeing the scene, and every branch of dialogue costs money whether or not most players hear it. Delivery carries information text cannot: hesitation, contempt, exhaustion. Lip-sync, subtitles and localisation all attach to the same asset, which is why voiced games ship with far larger content pipelines than their word counts suggest.

Origin Systems shipped Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger in 1994 with a fully performed cast, taking advantage of CD-ROM capacity and the studio's existing appetite for filmed material. Credit is shared rather than exclusive: several CD-ROM titles were adding speech in the same window, and arcade and adventure games had been using recorded lines in smaller quantities for years. What was new was voicing a long branching script end to end.

Consequences cut both ways. Performance raised the emotional ceiling and made silent protagonists feel like an authorial choice rather than a default, but it also froze scripts early, made late revisions expensive, and pushed studios toward fewer, shorter lines. Games with enormous branching text have often stayed partly voiced for exactly this reason, and a few have made a virtue of it by voicing only a narrator or a signature character.
f_voice_acting.spread: Metal Gear Solid directed its cast like radio drama, Baldur's Gate voiced only key lines, Bastion narrated play as it happened, and Disco Elysium voiced a novel's worth of text.
f_voice_acting.question: Which game was the first to be fully voice acted?

f_companion_approval.lede: Companion approval gives each party member a private opinion of the player that rises and falls with choices, gating conversations, side quests, romances and sometimes whether they stay at all.
body: Each recruitable character carries a hidden number. Dialogue choices, quest outcomes and even which companions you bring along nudge it up or down, and crossing a threshold unlocks a personal quest, a confession, a romance, or a departure in the middle of an act. Because the value is usually invisible, players read approval through reaction lines, which turns companions into ongoing puzzles rather than static bundles of statistics and equipment.

BioWare added the system to Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn in 2000 to fix a problem left by its predecessor, whose party was six competent mercenaries with no interior life. Giving each companion opinions, quarrels and a personal storyline made recruitment a choice about company rather than about statistics. It also cost little structurally, since approval is a counter attached to dialogue nodes the studio was already writing.

Approval turned party members into the reason many people replay, and it introduced a durable design problem at the same time. Optimising affection encourages players to answer as they believe a character wants rather than as they mean, and writers have responded by hiding the meter, adding companions who dislike flattery, or letting relationships simply fail. Romance content in particular draws criticism for treating intimacy as a lock with a known key.
f_companion_approval.spread: Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic tied approval to alignment, Dragon Age: Origins let companions leave outright, and Baldur's Gate 3 had them react to nearly every scene.
f_companion_approval.question: Which game invented companion approval ratings?

f_faction_rep.lede: Faction reputation tracks standing with each group in the world separately, so helping one side costs you with another and the question becomes whose side you are on, not whether you are good.
body: Every organisation keeps its own ledger. Kills, thefts, completed contracts and dialogue choices move a value attached to that faction, and the value drives concrete world state: guards who attack on sight, merchants who refuse to trade, quests that appear or vanish, safe passage through a district. Many systems propagate standing across alliances and rivalries, so a favour done for one militia automatically damages your position with the group it fights.

Interplay Productions built the system into Fallout in 1997 for a setting with no clear heroes. Its wasteland was full of settlements with incompatible interests, and a single morality score could not express the difference between raiders, a merchant town and a cult. Standing per group also made the world legible without a narrator, because a player can infer a faction's politics from what it rewards and what it punishes.

Splitting morality into constituencies solved the optimisation problem only partly. Players still maximise standing wherever they can, but the choices now trade against each other, and a world state that visibly diverges is harder to fake than a slider. Costs land on content: every faction needs writing, quests and an ending, and testing has to cover players who have made themselves hostile to everyone. Irreversible lockouts remain a common complaint.
f_faction_rep.spread: The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind used guild rank as advancement, Fallout: New Vegas made standing the plot, and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl let rival groups fight without the player.
f_faction_rep.question: Which game invented faction reputation systems?

f_karma_consequence.lede: A consequential branching endgame reshapes the final act of a game according to choices accumulated across the whole playthrough, rather than reporting them in text after the credits begin.
body: Decisions are recorded as flags and totals during play, then read at a branch point late in the story. What changes is structural: which levels exist, who fights beside you, which characters are alive, what the last confrontation is even about. That costs more than a slideshow epilogue, because it means building content most players will never see, and it forces writers to keep every thread resolvable from several incompatible states.

BioWare shipped Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic in 2003 with two substantially different final acts, driven by alignment and companion standing built up over dozens of hours. Doing so made the morality score mechanically honest: a number that had mostly bought powers now determined the shape of the ending. Working inside a licence helped, since it supplied two destinations audiences already understood, which kept the branching to a manageable width.

Once endings could genuinely diverge, players began treating earlier choices as investments, which raised the stakes of ordinary conversations and created a lasting expectation that games remember. Critics note how often the divergence is narrower than advertised, with branches reconverging on the same boss fight under different lighting. Studios have answered by branching smaller and more often, or by paying for genuinely different final hours and accepting that most players see one.
f_karma_consequence.spread: Fallout: New Vegas rebuilt its last battle around faction choice, Mass Effect 3 imported decisions from earlier games, and Undertale changed what the ending knew about you.
f_karma_consequence.question: Which game first let player choices change the whole ending?

f_dialogue_wheel.lede: A cinematic dialogue wheel replaces written reply options with short paraphrases arranged radially by tone, letting the player pick an intent quickly while the camera keeps moving through the scene.
body: Options sit at fixed compass positions, and position carries meaning: agreeable replies cluster on one side, aggressive ones on another, with investigative questions kept apart from choices that end the scene. Each label is a summary rather than the line itself, so the player commits to a tone and the actor supplies the words. Timers are common, and choosing early lets the response interrupt instead of waiting politely for silence.

Mass Effect used the wheel in 2007 so that conversations could be shot like film. BioWare wanted scenes staged with moving cameras and performed by voiced actors on both sides, which is incompatible with a player who stops to read four complete sentences. Consistent positions meant regulars could choose almost without reading, and paraphrasing let the writers make spoken lines longer and stranger than any menu entry could be.

Trading precision for continuity carries a well-documented cost. Paraphrases sometimes misrepresent what the character then says, and the spatial layout encourages players to pick a side of the wheel early and stay there, flattening performance into a personality setting. Defenders argue the wheel is what made dialogue watchable rather than readable, and therefore the only reason conversation survived the move to fully staged cinematic scenes.
f_dialogue_wheel.spread: Mass Effect 2 attached interrupts to the wheel's edges, Fallout 4 compressed it to four terse options, and Assassin's Creed Odyssey used it to voice two different protagonists.
f_dialogue_wheel.question: Which game invented the dialogue wheel?

f_agency_twist.lede: A player-agency narrative twist turns the story onto the player's own obedience, revealing that doing as you were told was the subject of the game rather than the way through it.
body: Structure carries the trick. For most of its length the game trains a habit, usually compliance with an authoritative voice issuing objectives, and rewards that habit exactly as any game would. Late on, the fiction reframes the habit as characterisation, so the player's behaviour becomes evidence about the player. Done properly it requires no new systems at all, only the discipline to make obedience the one thing never questioned along the way.

Irrational Games staged the device in BioShock in 2007, using a phrase repeated by a friendly radio voice to mark every instruction the player had followed without thinking. Its precondition was a decade of first-person games teaching people that objectives arrive over the radio and are obeyed. Environmental storytelling supplied the other half, since the world had to hold enough evidence for the reveal to look inevitable in hindsight.

Turning interactivity into theme gave the medium an argument no other form can make, and it is close to unrepeatable. Once players expect the twist, the trained habit is no longer sincere, so later games have had to earn the effect differently: by making refusal possible, by tracking whether you quit, or by addressing you directly. Sceptics observe that the twist frequently criticises linearity while remaining entirely linear itself.
f_agency_twist.spread: The Stanley Parable made disobedience the system itself, Undertale remembered restarts, BioShock Infinite recast the twist as determinism, and Deltarune returned to asking who is choosing.
f_agency_twist.question: Which game turned player obedience into a plot twist?

f_hitpoints.lede: Hit points express a character's remaining capacity to absorb damage as a depleting number, so a blow reduces a pool instead of instantly ending the fight or the life.
body: Damage becomes arithmetic. Attacks subtract a value, healing adds one, zero means death, and nearly everything else in the design hangs off that single scalar: difficulty tuning, item pricing, monster placement, the pacing of a dungeon. Because the pool is just a number it can also be displayed as a bar, capped, regenerated, or grown with experience, and most combat systems since have been built by attaching further rules to it.

Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold gave Rogue hit points around 1980, inheriting them wholesale from tabletop role-playing rules that had circulated since the mid-1970s. Credit is properly shared: the idea predates the medium, and other early mainframe dungeon games used the same borrowed arithmetic. What Rogue contributed was pairing the pool with permadeath and randomly generated floors, where a shrinking number becomes a running judgement about how much further you dare go.

Quantifying survival turned combat into a negotiation rather than a coin flip, which is what made difficulty tunable at all. It also imported an odd model of injury, in which a character at one hit point fights exactly as well as one at full health, and it rewards attrition play that designers have fought ever since with stamina bars, wound states, armour layers and regeneration. Every alternative is still measured against it.
f_hitpoints.spread: The Legend of Zelda displayed them as hearts, Street Fighter II drained a visible bar against a clock, and Diablo turned the pool into one more stat to optimise.
f_hitpoints.question: Which game first used hit points?

f_combo_string.lede: Chained combo strings are attack sequences timed so each hit lands while the opponent is still reeling from the last, making the rest of the run unblockable once the first connects.
body: Hit reaction is the mechanism. A connecting attack puts the target in a stun state lasting a fixed number of frames, and an attack begun inside that window arrives before the defender regains control. Chaining therefore depends on frame data rather than on any dedicated combo mode, and skill lies in knowing which moves recover fast enough to link, which is why the technique produced deep, memorised notation among competitive players.

Capcom did not design it. While finishing Street Fighter II: The World Warrior in 1991 the team noticed that cancelling the recovery of one move into another let hits connect in sequence, judged the timing too demanding for most players to exploit, and left it alone. Players found it within weeks. Combos consequently arrived as a discovered property of the engine rather than a feature, which is unusually well documented for a bug.

Strings gave fighting games a skill ceiling nobody had authored, splitting the audience between players who drill execution and players who do not, and setting off thirty years of balancing between them. Outside the genre, the same idea became the grammar of character action games, skateboarding scoring and superhero brawlers, where a string matters less for damage than for rhythm and spectacle. Combo breakers and bursts have been arriving ever since.
f_combo_string.spread: Tekken rebuilt strings for 3D movement, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater scored them as trick lines, Devil May Cry graded style, and Batman: Arkham Asylum turned them into rhythm.
f_combo_string.question: Which game invented combos in fighting games?

f_cancel_meter.lede: Cancels and a super meter let a player interrupt one move's animation with another and bank a resource earned through fighting, spending it on a decisive attack at a chosen moment.
body: Two rules work together. Cancelling permits a move still in its animation to be overridden by another input, which is what makes long strings possible; the meter fills as you attack, block and take damage, and empties when spent on a special that is faster, safer or far more damaging. Because the bar is visible to both players, everyone watching the cabinet can see when a round has turned dangerous.

Capcom formalised the pairing in Super Street Fighter II Turbo, after players had spent years exploiting cancels the studio never intended. Attribution is shared rather than clean: SNK fighters of the early 1990s had already experimented with drainable spirit gauges, and competing arcade boards were converging on similar ideas. What Capcom fixed in place was the loop in which playing well earns the resource that ends the round.

Meters gave the genre its comeback drama and much of its spectator legibility, which matters for a form watched over a shoulder or on a stream. They also shifted matches toward resource management, so a player behind on health may be ahead on options, and they made balance considerably harder, since a single meter-spending move has to be worth its cost without erasing the preceding two minutes of play.
f_cancel_meter.spread: Street Fighter III: New Generation let players pick which super to carry, and The King of Fighters '94 built its own charge-and-spend economy alongside team selection.
f_cancel_meter.question: Which game introduced the super meter in fighting games?

f_parry_riposte.lede: A parry and riposte window rewards deflecting an incoming attack within a few frames, converting a successful defence into a guaranteed counterattack rather than a safe but passive block.
body: Timing is everything. Pressing the defensive input just before contact triggers a state that negates damage and leaves the attacker exposed for a fixed period, long enough to guarantee a punish. Missing the window normally leaves the defender open instead, which is exactly the point: a parry is a bet that you know what is coming. Systems differ in how wide the window is and whether repeated attempts carry any risk.

Capcom introduced the parry in Street Fighter III: New Generation in 1997, at a moment when the studio wanted to reset a genre it had defined and to reward reading an opponent over drilling strings. Defence had been the dull half of fighting games, and making it an aggressive act with a price restored the guessing game. Earlier titles had counter moves, but the frame-tight window with an assured reply is what survived.

Migration out of fighting games was rapid and close to total. Parrying gives action, stealth and role-playing designers a way to make dangerous enemies fair without lowering their damage, since the player always has an answer that depends on attention rather than statistics. Costs are real: a strong parry can flatten a combat system into one correct verb, and players who cannot hit the timing get locked out of content the design assumes is reachable.
f_parry_riposte.spread: Bloodborne parried with a gunshot, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice made deflection the default, Cuphead parried pink objects for meter, and Ghost of Tsushima taught it through duels.
f_parry_riposte.question: Which game invented the parry window?

f_directional_block.lede: Directional attack and block give strikes and guards a spatial orientation, so an overhead cut has to be met with a high guard and reading the angle matters as much as reacting to the timing.
body: Geometry replaces a single block button. Each attack carries a direction, high, low, left or right, and the defender picks a matching stance or guard; a mismatch lets the blow through or trades badly. Stance systems extend the idea by grouping moves under postures with different coverage, so choosing a stance is a standing prediction about what the opponent intends rather than a moment-to-moment reaction to what they do.

Light Weight built Bushido Blade in 1997 around the argument that sword fights end quickly. Discarding health bars in favour of limb damage and lethal strikes made blocking a question of where the blade is rather than how much damage remains, and a directional guard was the only way to express that with a controller. Its immediate ancestors are the fighting game combo systems it was deliberately rejecting.

Melee as reading rather than execution has persisted, mostly in third-person action games that want swordplay to feel like an argument between two people. Adoption stayed narrow because the scheme needs either many buttons or an analogue stick the camera also wants, and because directional guessing frustrates players who cannot see a wind-up clearly. Motion controls and stance systems are two different answers to that same input problem.
f_directional_block.spread: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword mapped the angle onto a motion controller, and Ghost of Tsushima folded the idea into stances chosen against different enemy weapons.
f_directional_block.question: Which game introduced directional blocking in sword combat?

f_weapon_durability.lede: Weapon durability decay makes equipment wear out with use, so tools become consumables on a budget rather than permanent possessions and the player keeps replacing whatever they fight with.
body: Each item carries a use counter. Swinging, firing or blocking decrements it, and at zero the item breaks or becomes useless, sometimes with repair available at a price. Design consequences follow immediately: inventory turns into rotating stock rather than a museum, powerful finds get spent instead of hoarded, and a designer can hand the player something extraordinary without permanently flattening the difficulty curve behind it.

Intelligent Systems shipped Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light in 1990 with durability because its units die permanently and its weapons form a triangle of counters. Limited uses stopped players solving every map with one legendary sword and forced rotation through characters and armaments. Constraint suited a strategy game in which each battle is a resource problem inside a campaign that never returns anything you spend.

Durability is among the most reliably disliked systems in the medium and among the most useful. Breakage creates improvisation, prevents hoarding, and keeps a difficulty curve honest; it also generates busywork, punishes attachment, and encourages players to save their best equipment for a moment that never comes. Where it works, replacement is fast and generous. Where it fails, repair becomes a chore performed in menus between fights.
f_weapon_durability.spread: Far Cry 2 jammed rusting rifles mid-fight, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild made breakage the rhythm of exploration, and Monster Hunter 4 tied blade sharpness to it.
f_weapon_durability.question: Which game invented weapon durability?

f_ability_cooldown.lede: An ability cooldown economy gates powers by time rather than by a resource pool, so each skill returns after a fixed wait and play gets organised around recharging clocks.
body: Every ability owns a timer. Using it starts a countdown during which the button does nothing, and the real decisions concern sequencing: which skill to spend now, which to hold for a moment that will matter more, how to cover the gap while the strong option recharges. Unlike mana, cooldowns cannot be stockpiled, so power output is capped per minute rather than per expedition.

Verant Interactive leaned on timers in EverQuest in 1999 because a persistent shared world needs rate limits that a single-player game does not. Mana alone lets a well-supplied player unload everything at once, which breaks group encounters and server economies alike, while a clock throttles output regardless of how many potions someone brought. Timed abilities also gave each class a rhythm that other players could learn and depend on.

Scheduling became the shape of combat, which is why cooldowns underpin team games where readable, predictable power is essential; watching an opponent's timers is itself a competitive skill. Costs include rotation play, in which optimal use degenerates into repeating a memorised sequence, and a peculiar fiction where a hero cannot swing the same sword the same way twice within ten seconds for reasons the world never explains.
f_ability_cooldown.spread: World of Warcraft built class rotations on them, League of Legends made cooldown reduction a stat to buy, and Overwatch reduced whole characters to three timed abilities.
f_ability_cooldown.question: Which game popularised ability cooldowns?

f_bullet_time.lede: Player-controlled bullet time slows the game clock on demand while leaving aiming at full speed, letting the player spend a limited resource to buy accuracy inside a chaotic firefight.
body: Simulation and input run at different rates. Activating the effect scales physics, animation and projectile speed down while camera and cursor stay responsive, so the player perceives more time to decide than the characters have. A drainable meter limits abuse, and the state is usually entered through a dive or a roll that commits the character to a trajectory, which stops slow motion from being a free pause button.

Remedy Entertainment made it the core verb of Max Payne in 2001, borrowing the visual grammar of contemporary action cinema and discovering that the technique also solved a control problem. A mouse can aim precisely, but a room with several armed men gives no time to use that precision, so slowing the world converted a twitch test into a planning exercise while keeping the player's hands busy throughout.

Directorial control over your own action scene proved appealing enough to become a convention, and it quietly works as an accessibility feature, since a slowed clock lowers the reaction speed a game demands without softening it in other respects. Overused, the effect drains tension: a player who can pause danger at will stops respecting it. Later designs answered by charging more for the privilege or by making time itself the puzzle.
f_bullet_time.spread: Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time rewound instead, Fallout 3 turned it into a targeting menu, Bayonetta earned it by dodging, and Superhot tied time to movement.
f_bullet_time.question: Which game invented bullet time?

f_regen_health.lede: Regenerating health restores a player's damage capacity automatically after a short period without being hit, replacing scavenged medical supplies with a rhythm of pressure, retreat and return.
body: Recovery lives on a timer, not in the inventory. Taking damage starts a delay; surviving that delay without further hits refills the pool, often only up to a segment boundary rather than to full. Implementations differ in whether the regenerating layer is a shield sitting over a fixed health bar or the health itself, and in how loudly the interface screams as you approach death, which does most of the work.

Bungie shipped Halo: Combat Evolved in 2001 with a recharging shield above a conventional health bar, chosen partly to make a console shooter playable with a controller and partly to keep encounters flowing rather than ending in a hunt for medkits. Credit is contested in the details: fully regenerating health with no pickups at all arrived in later shooters, including Bungie's own sequel, so 2001 is the hinge rather than the finish.

Level design changed more than combat did. Arenas replaced corridors, cover placement became a pacing tool, and designers stopped distributing health as a currency across a map, which removed a resource layer and a reason to explore at the same time. Critics blame regeneration for a decade of shooters that reward hiding behind a wall until the screen clears; defenders note it made large, forgiving encounters possible on a gamepad.
f_regen_health.spread: Halo 2 dropped the separate health bar, Gears of War paired it with cover, and Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare made a reddening screen the entire interface.
f_regen_health.question: Which game invented regenerating health?

f_two_weapon_limit.lede: A constrained weapon loadout limits the player to carrying two guns at once, so every pickup is a decision about what to abandon rather than an addition to an ever-growing arsenal.
body: Capacity is the whole constraint. With two slots, ammunition scarcity becomes meaningful, weapons can be tuned to fill distinct roles without redundancy, and a level designer can predict roughly what the player is holding on entering a room. Grenades and melee usually sit outside the limit so there is always an answer available, and discarded weapons stay on the ground as a visible, retrievable record of the choice.

Bungie adopted the rule for Halo: Combat Evolved in 2001, partly because a gamepad has nowhere to put a nine-entry weapon wheel and partly because the studio wanted its sandbox readable. Two weapons bind to comfortable buttons and swap in a moment, and an encounter can then be built on the assumption that the player carries one long-range and one close-range option, or has already made a mistake.

Limiting the loadout gave console shooters a clarity their inventory-heavy predecessors lacked, and it pushed level design toward supplying the right weapon near the moment it is needed. Losses are equally clear: the walking-armoury fantasy disappears, experimentation carries a cost, and players who enjoy hoarding find the rule stingy. Games have argued the point ever since, some shipping both schemes and letting the audience pick.
f_two_weapon_limit.spread: Halo 2 added dual wielding within the limit, Halo 3: ODST rebuilt encounters around scarcity, and BioShock Infinite applied the rule to a game already full of powers.
f_two_weapon_limit.question: Which game started the two-weapon limit in shooters?

f_cover_system.lede: A snap-to-cover system lets the player attach to walls and low barriers with a button, sliding along protection and firing from behind it without exposing the whole body.
body: Geometry becomes a verb. Pressing the cover button binds the character to a surface, switching camera and controls: movement slides along the wall, aiming pops out at marked corners, and blind fire trades accuracy for safety. Level layouts therefore encode a combat script in advance, since designers place chest-high objects to define lanes, flanking routes and the distance at which a fight is meant to be fought.

Namco released kill.switch in 2003 with the mechanic in recognisably modern form, built on the over-the-shoulder camera that arrived around the same time. Priority is genuinely contested: earlier third-person shooters had let players press against walls to peek, and light-gun games had used duck-and-shoot cover for years. What 2003 assembled was the specific combination of shoulder camera, dedicated cover button and levels designed entirely around both.

Cover made third-person gunfights readable and handed designers precise control over pacing, which is why it dominated a console generation. Cost arrived as sameness: once the system exists, every arena drifts toward the same scattering of waist-high concrete, and enemies must be written to flush the player out or fights stall. Later designs kept the camera and loosened the attachment, preferring cover that gets used rather than entered.
f_cover_system.spread: Gears of War made it the genre template, Uncharted 2: Among Thieves ran it through collapsing scenery, and Mass Effect 2 fused it with recharging powers.
f_cover_system.question: Which game invented the cover system?

f_recoil_pattern.lede: Learnable recoil patterns make a weapon's spray deterministic, so a held trigger climbs and drifts the same way every time and players can cancel it with a memorised mouse movement.
body: Randomness is removed, or nearly. Each successive shot in a burst is displaced by a fixed offset, producing a repeatable path that players learn to draw in the air and then counter by pulling along its inverse. Accuracy penalties for moving and jumping complete the system, because the pattern only holds while standing still, which turns every engagement into a decision about whether to stop moving.

Counter-Strike began in 1999 as a Half-Life modification by Minh Le and Jess Cliffe, and its weapon handling reflected a preference for consistency over realism: a fight decided by a random number generator cannot be studied. Deterministic spray gave the mod a skill that could be practised alone, which suited the competitive scene forming around it, and later official releases preserved the patterns almost as inherited law.

Fixed patterns create an invisible skill curve, unmentioned in tutorials and enormous in effect, which explains part of the steep gradient between new and practised players in competitive shooters. That opacity is also the standard criticism, since a mechanic nobody explains functions as a barrier; studios have since added practice ranges and visible spray previews. Alternatives that randomise more are usually judged less fair rather than more.
f_recoil_pattern.spread: Counter-Strike: Source inherited the patterns nearly intact, Valorant gave every weapon its own studied curve, and Escape from Tarkov modelled recoil through weapon attachments.
f_recoil_pattern.question: Which game introduced learnable recoil patterns?

f_stamina.lede: A stamina action economy draws every attack, dodge, sprint and block from one shared bar that refills slowly, so committing to an action means being briefly unable to take another.
body: One bar governs offence and defence alike. Each action deducts a cost, regeneration pauses while acting and often while guarding, and an empty bar leaves the character standing still through whatever happens next. Weight, armour and equipment adjust costs and recovery, so build decisions are really decisions about how many actions per second a character can afford against a particular enemy.

FromSoftware built the economy into Demon's Souls in 2009 to make combat deliberate while action games were accelerating around it. Stamina meters long predate the game, in sports titles and earlier action games, so the innovation was not the bar but its scope. Making every verb draw from a single pool converts panic into a punishable state and forces players to decide, before swinging, whether they can afford to be wrong.

Deliberateness became a genre. Since the bar is visible and enemy attack rhythms are legible, fights turn into questions of spacing and patience rather than reflex, and difficulty can be raised without inflating damage numbers. Costs include a certain sameness of pace and real frustration when the bar denies an escape the player could clearly see coming. Several later designs restrict stamina to sprinting and leave combat free.
f_stamina.spread: Dark Souls made the bar a genre signature, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild spent it on climbing, and Death Stranding spent it on staying upright while walking.
f_stamina.question: Which game made stamina the core of melee combat?

f_poise_stagger.lede: Poise and stagger break give characters a second, hidden bar that absorbs the impact of blows, and emptying it leaves them reeling and open to a heavy punishing attack.
body: Impact is tracked separately from damage. Every hit carries a poise value alongside its damage value, and landing hits faster than the target's poise regenerates eventually breaks it, producing a stagger animation and a window for a decisive strike. Armour and weight raise the threshold, letting heavily equipped characters swing through incoming blows without flinching, which turns equipment choice into a question of who interrupts whom.

FromSoftware introduced it alongside stamina in Demon's Souls in 2009 to answer a problem the stamina bar creates. If defence is cheap and attacks are slow, patient play degenerates into waiting indefinitely, so a second bar rewards sustained pressure and punishes players who never commit. Keeping the value invisible was deliberate: balance is read from animation and sound rather than from a number sitting on the screen.

Aggression against patience became a genuine dilemma rather than a stylistic preference, which is the mechanical core of the soulslike. Hidden bars carry costs, though: without a readout, players learn thresholds by repetition, and complaints about poise values have followed the genre through every entry, with numbers rewritten between patches. Later games made the bar visible on bosses, trading some of the mystery for legibility.
f_poise_stagger.spread: Dark Souls tuned poise around armour weight, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice turned the bar into the win condition, and Elden Ring made staggering bosses a whole build goal.
f_poise_stagger.question: Which game introduced poise and stagger in melee combat?

f_execution_finisher.lede: A contextual execution is a scripted close-range kill triggered against a weakened or unaware enemy, trading a moment of vulnerability and lost control for a burst of animated spectacle.
body: Conditions gate the move. An enemy has to be downed, stunned or unaware, and standing in the right place surfaces a prompt; pressing it hands control to a fixed animation lasting a second or two. Through that window the player usually cannot move, dodge or shoot, so the cost is exposure to everyone else in the room, and generous designs pay it back with ammunition, health or a broken enemy formation.

Epic Games put executions into Gears of War in 2006, where they suited a design already built on downed enemies, heavy characters and a camera pinned close behind the shoulder. Cover shooting had made firefights static, so a violent, committed close-range option gave players a reason to leave the wall. Spectacle mattered commercially too, since a launch title on new hardware is bought partly for what it looks like.

Executions solved a real pacing problem by punctuating repetitive combat with a beat of closure, and they became the standard reward for successful stealth and crowd control. Criticism has settled on repetition, because the same animation on its hundredth viewing is a delay rather than a flourish, and on tone, because the design asks players to seek out cruelty for a bonus. Skippable finishers are now common.
f_execution_finisher.spread: Dead Space made dismemberment the whole system, Batman: Arkham Asylum used them to end fights cleanly, Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor made them personal, and Dishonored offered non-lethal versions.
f_execution_finisher.question: Which game popularised contextual execution moves?

f_gear_swap_combat.lede: Deflect-focused posture combat replaces dodging with well-timed deflection, filling an opponent's posture bar until their guard breaks, so duels are won by holding rhythm rather than by managing distance.
body: Victory runs through the posture bar, not the health bar. Blocking adds posture damage, deflecting adds far more and costs the defender almost nothing, and a broken guard opens a lethal blow regardless of remaining health. Retreating lets an opponent recover, which inverts the usual advice; safe play means staying in range and meeting attacks on the beat, with unblockable moves forcing a different answer at intervals.

FromSoftware built Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice in 2019 from two of its own inheritances, the parry window fighting games had refined since the late 1990s and the stagger bar the studio introduced a decade earlier. Removing character builds and equipment scaling made the change workable: with no statistics to hide behind, timing becomes the only variable, and difficulty can be tuned entirely through enemy rhythm and recovery.

Combat moved closer to a rhythm game than a spacing game, which produced both the design's admirers and its detractors. Players who internalise the beat describe the most legible melee system in the genre; players who cannot find it have no alternative route, because there is nothing to overlevel. That absence of a fallback is the honest cost of taking statistics out of a difficulty curve entirely.
f_gear_swap_combat.spread: Lies of P charged perfect guards against weapon durability, and Wo Long: Fallen Dynasty rebuilt the idea around deflecting flagged critical attacks during large group fights.
f_gear_swap_combat.question: Which game made deflection the core of its combat?

f_ragdoll.lede: Ragdoll physics simulate a body as jointed rigid parts once it loses control, so falls and deaths are computed from momentum and collision rather than played back from a fixed animation.
body: A skeleton is rebuilt as physics objects. Limbs become rigid bodies joined by constraints that roughly match human range of motion, and when the game hands control to the solver the body falls under gravity, catching on stairs and railings on the way down. Results are unrepeatable by construction, which is both the appeal and the problem: no two deaths look alike, and none can be art-directed in advance.

DreamWorks Interactive shipped Jurassic Park: Trespasser in 1998 with an unusually ambitious full-body simulation, and it was widely judged a failure at the time, its arm controls and unstable bodies becoming a standing joke. Credit is therefore awkward: the technique only became reliable in other studios' hands a few years later. What Trespasser demonstrated, expensively, was that simulated bodies had become computationally possible on consumer machines.

Simulation replaced animation for one narrow case and changed how worlds felt, because a body that interacts with geometry is evidence that the geometry is real. It also introduced a permanent tonal risk, since physics has no sense of occasion: corpses flail, catch on doorframes and slide downhill, and a solemn death becomes slapstick. Most games now blend authored animation with simulation to keep some control over the moment.
f_ragdoll.spread: Max Payne let bodies fall through its slow motion, Half-Life 2 made them part of puzzles, Just Cause 2 built stunts on them, and Fall Guys made flailing the point.
f_ragdoll.question: Which game first used ragdoll physics?

f_rigid_body_puzzle.lede: Rigid-body puzzle physics turn mass, buoyancy and leverage into the vocabulary of a puzzle, so solutions get built by stacking, floating and tipping objects the simulation handles consistently.
body: Objects carry properties the player can learn. Weight decides whether a crate holds a seesaw down, density decides what floats, friction decides whether a ramp works, and the same rules apply in every room. Puzzles are then authored as situations rather than as locks: a designer arranges materials and a goal, and any arrangement of forces that reaches the goal counts as a legitimate solution.

Valve released Half-Life 2 in 2004 with a licensed physics engine wired into level design instead of into decoration. Its early chapters work as a tutorial in the rules, teaching buoyancy with barrels and leverage with planks before asking players to combine them. Processing cost had fallen far enough by then to run consistent rigid-body simulation alongside a shooter, which is why 2004 rather than 1998 is the hinge here.

Physics as a solution space made worlds feel governed by law rather than by script, and gave designers puzzles that tolerate improvisation. Reliability is the recurring difficulty: simulations drift, objects clip through geometry, and a puzzle with many valid answers also has many failure states in which the crate you needed has bounced somewhere unreachable. Most games manage that risk by bolting crucial objects into fixed positions.
f_rigid_body_puzzle.spread: Portal built momentum puzzles on it, World of Goo made structures from it, Angry Birds sold it as demolition, and Tears of the Kingdom let players assemble machines.
f_rigid_body_puzzle.question: Which game made physics the basis of its puzzles?

f_physics_tool.lede: A physics manipulation tool is an in-game device that lets the player grab, hold and launch simulated objects directly, turning an abstract system into something you point at the world.
body: Interaction is mediated by a single object. Holding the trigger picks up whatever the reticle covers and keeps it suspended at a fixed distance; releasing drops it, and a second input fires it with force. Because the tool works on anything the simulation owns, it doubles as a teaching device, giving players a safe way to discover mass, fragility and reaction before that knowledge is required to progress.

Valve introduced the gravity gun in Half-Life 2 in 2004, directly after chapters that had taught the underlying physics through seesaws and floating barrels. Handing players one tool that operates on those rules everywhere solved a discoverability problem, since a systemic world is worth nothing if nobody notices what is systemic. Putting it in the hands rather than in a menu also made the system feel like equipment instead of a mode.

One object can teach a whole system, and that lesson outlived the specific weapon. Later games hand out magnet tools, freeze rays and telekinesis for the same reason, and virtual reality made direct grabbing the default rather than a special item. Risks are familiar: a strong manipulation tool trivialises puzzles that assumed walking, and it encourages players to carry a solved solution into the next room.
f_physics_tool.spread: Portal replaced it with portals and momentum, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild split it into magnesis and stasis, and Half-Life: Alyx gave grabbing to the hands.
f_physics_tool.question: Which game invented the gravity gun?

f_destructible.lede: Destructible geometry lets players remove or collapse parts of a level's structure during play, so walls, floors and cover become consumable terrain rather than the fixed boundaries of a designed space.
body: Level surfaces become mutable. Explosives and heavy weapons carve holes, remove supports or delete whole sections, and the game recomputes navigation, line of sight and collision to match. Approaches range from fully deformable geometry to pre-authored breakable pieces that swap in damaged versions, and most shipping games use the second, because it is predictable, cheap to compute and far kinder to multiplayer synchronisation.

Volition shipped Red Faction in 2001 with technology that let players tunnel through rock and blow doorways in walls, marketed openly as the reason the game existed. Its appeal was contrarian: a shooter promising to undermine every assumption a level designer makes about where players will be. Hardware of the period could only support the effect in specific materials, so the freedom was noticeably bounded in practice.

Losing the guarantee of a fixed floor plan is exactly why destruction stays attractive and why it is used sparingly. Breakable walls make cover temporary, defeat memorised map knowledge, and hand players tools designers cannot anticipate; they also break pathfinding, complicate network code, and can leave a match in a bowl of rubble with nothing left to hide behind. Modern designs usually destroy surfaces while preserving structure.
f_destructible.spread: Battlefield: Bad Company 2 removed cover a wall at a time, Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege made breaching the tactical core, and The Finals built whole matches around collapse.
f_destructible.question: Which game invented destructible environments?

f_voxel_terrain.lede: Editable voxel terrain models the world as a uniform grid of blocks that can each be removed or placed, making landscape a material the player edits rather than a surface they cross.
body: Everything is cells. Each grid position holds a material identifier or nothing at all, the renderer builds visible surfaces from the boundaries between them, and mining and building are simply writes into that array. Uniformity is where the power comes from: physics, lighting, storage, generation and network synchronisation all operate on one simple structure, and a rule written for one block type applies across the entire world.

Markus Persson began Minecraft in 2009 after playing Infiniminer, an earlier block-mining game whose grid he has repeatedly credited as the direct inspiration. Mojang's contribution was to attach survival, crafting and generation to that grid so editing terrain became a means rather than an end. Voxel representations themselves are much older, used in medical imaging and earlier terrain renderers, so the novelty lay in the design around them.

Uniform editable matter turned out to be the most generative world model the medium has found, because one mechanic supports mining, building, farming, traps, circuitry and art with no special cases. Costs are aesthetic and computational: everything is cubic unless considerable work goes into hiding it, and worlds of any size demand chunked streaming, level-of-detail tricks and hard limits on how much may change at once.
f_voxel_terrain.spread: Terraria applied the grid to a two-dimensional world, and Deep Rock Galactic used fully carvable caves to make procedurally generated terrain the actual object of the job.
f_voxel_terrain.question: Which game made the world out of editable blocks?

f_soft_body.lede: Soft-body deformation simulates a structure as a flexible network of connected nodes, so an object bends, crumples and tears according to force rather than switching to a pre-made damaged model.
body: Objects are built from nodes and beams. Each node carries mass and position, each beam carries stiffness and a breaking threshold, and the solver resolves forces between them many times per second, so a collision propagates through the structure as deformation instead of a swapped mesh. Damage is continuous and cumulative: a bent chassis stays bent, wheels misalign, and handling degrades in ways nobody authored in advance.

BeamNG GmbH released BeamNG.drive into early access in 2013 with soft-body simulation as the entire product, descending from the ragdoll work of the late 1990s but applied to vehicles rather than corpses. Timing came down to processing budget, since solving thousands of constrained nodes in real time only became feasible on ordinary multi-core desktop hardware, and even then the simulation costs far more than the graphics around it.

Fidelity here buys spectacle and study rather than gameplay, which is why the technique has stayed specialised. Crash behaviour that follows from physics is compelling to watch and genuinely useful to engineering-minded players, but it complicates everything a conventional game wants: predictable difficulty, repeatable encounters, network synchronisation and a performance budget shared with other systems. Racing games mostly still swap damage models instead.
f_soft_body.spread: Nothing here inherits it: BeamNG.drive remains the reference implementation, while mainstream racing games continue to swap pre-authored damage models rather than simulate deformation directly.
f_soft_body.question: Which game simulates car crashes with soft-body physics?

f_vehicle_sim.lede: High-fidelity vehicle physics model tyre grip, weight transfer and drivetrain behaviour closely enough that driving becomes a skill of managing load, and tuning a car matters as much as steering it.
body: Grip is computed, not assigned. A tyre model converts load, slip angle and surface into force, weight shifts between wheels under braking and cornering, and the drivetrain decides which wheels receive torque, so identical inputs produce different results depending on what the car was doing a moment earlier. Setup values such as gearing, downforce and suspension stiffness feed the same equations, which is what makes tuning consequential.

Polyphony Digital shipped Gran Turismo in 1997 on hardware finally able to run that arithmetic per wheel at frame rate, and paired it with licensed production cars and a career built on buying and modifying them. Serious simulation had existed on personal computers for years in specialist titles, so what 1997 established was that a mass console audience would accept a demanding physical model if the surrounding game was about ownership.

Racing became an equipment hobby, complete with tuning forums, driving-line theory and eventually consumer wheels and pedals, while the same physics work later served open-world games where cars are transport rather than sport. Realism cuts against accessibility, so most series ship assists that quietly simplify the model underneath, and the argument about how much simulation a general audience actually wants has never been settled.
f_vehicle_sim.spread: Gran Turismo 3: A-Spec refined the model on faster hardware, Need for Speed: Underground traded it for arcade tuning culture, and Rocket League applied car physics to football.
f_vehicle_sim.question: Which game brought realistic driving physics to consoles?

f_flight_sim.lede: Flight simulation models aerodynamics, instruments and navigation for their own sake, offering no score and no enemy, on the argument that operating the aircraft correctly is itself the entertainment.
body: Systems are the content. Lift and drag respond to airspeed and attitude, instruments read from the simulated state rather than from a heads-up display, and a flight consists of checklists, navigation between real airfields, radio procedure and a landing that either works or does not. Failure is rarely dramatic; it is being lost, low on fuel, or descending at a rate the airframe will not forgive.

subLOGIC's product line reached IBM personal computers as Microsoft Flight Simulator 1.0 in 1982, though the lineage runs back further, through earlier subLOGIC releases on 8-bit home machines and flight models written for mainframes. Choosing an unscored simulation was partly a hardware argument: drawing a wireframe world and integrating flight equations consumed everything the machine had, leaving nothing for adversaries or scoring systems.

Simulation as its own reward established a whole branch of the medium, with a hardware ecosystem of yokes and pedals and an audience that treats fidelity as the review criterion. That audience is also a constraint, because every increase in realism narrows the potential player base. Its tradition has survived through study-level products and by supplying the flight models that action games then simplify for everyone else.
f_flight_sim.spread: Wing Commander wrapped a flight model in melodrama, Star Wars: TIE Fighter used it for scripted campaigns, and Kerbal Space Program applied the same rigour to orbital mechanics.
f_flight_sim.question: What was the first flight simulator game?

f_propagation_sim.lede: Propagating fire and fluids spread through a world according to wind, fuel and terrain, producing hazards that keep developing after the player starts them and that no designer scripted in advance.
body: Spread is simulated across a grid of flammable material.
