Games stopped being finished objects and became product lines, a shift that made long-lived franchises viable and gave studios work between releases. Fragmentation is one cost, as multiplayer populations split between owners and non-owners, and temptation is another, since content nearly complete at launch can always be held back. Every later model, from downloadable content to seasonal passes, argues with the precedent set here.
f_expansion_pack.spread: The Sims turned expansions into an annual line, RollerCoaster Tycoon added themed parks, and Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree delivered one region priced near a full game.
f_expansion_pack.question: What was the first video game expansion pack?

f_dlc.lede: Downloadable content delivers post-release additions over the network at any size, from a full campaign to a single cosmetic item, bought directly from a storefront built into the console or game.
body: Delivery rather than scope is the defining trait. Because distribution costs almost nothing, the unit of sale can be one texture or an entire region, and it arrives with no manufacturing, no retail and no box. Storefronts handle payment and entitlement, and the content either unlocks data already installed or downloads a patch. Bundles, seasons and staggered release schedules all follow from that flexibility.

Bethesda Game Studios sold a horse armour cosmetic for The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion in 2006 for a small sum, and the reaction taught the industry exactly how little could be packaged and sold. Consoles had experimented with downloadable additions earlier over dial-up and broadband services, so the technology was not new. New was the combination: a mainstream storefront, a connected installed base, and a public demonstration of the floor.

Revenue after launch became normal, which funds longer support for games and, in the same motion, makes it rational to plan a release around what will be withheld from it. Players learned to read a launch as provisional until the schedule appeared. Preservation suffers most, because content tied to a storefront disappears when that storefront does, and a delisted add-on can leave a game impossible to experience as sold.
f_dlc.spread: Rock Band ran a weekly song store, Grand Theft Auto IV shipped two episodic campaigns, and Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree used the format for a single expansion-sized region.
f_dlc.question: Which game started paid downloadable content?

f_season_pass.lede: A season pass sells future downloadable content before it exists, bundling an unspecified schedule of additions into one advance purchase priced below the sum of the individual parts.
body: Payment happens up front and delivery happens over months. What arrives is defined loosely, sometimes as a number of packs, sometimes as everything released within a window, and the buyer carries the risk on scope, quality and timing. Content unlocks automatically as it ships. Discounting against the sum of the parts is the compensation offered for buying something nobody has finished making.

Team Bondi's L.A. Noire carried an early example in 2011 and is the release usually credited with the term, though passes for episodic content and music packs appeared in the same period, which makes the attribution soft. Motivation was financial rather than creative. Revenue could be booked earlier, a committed audience could be sized before content existed, and the announced schedule became a marketing asset in itself.

Studios gained a funded runway for post-launch teams, which is a genuine benefit when the alternative is disbanding them the week after release. Trust pays for it. A pass whose contents disappoint or slip produces a specific kind of anger, and several publishers have cancelled or refunded them. Structurally the model also pushes announcements earlier, since what is being sold is a roadmap rather than a thing.
f_season_pass.spread: Battlefield 3 bundled map packs to keep its multiplayer population together, Halo 4 attached one to matchmaking playlists, and Destiny used a pass as scaffolding for its first year.
f_season_pass.question: Which game introduced the season pass?

f_f2p.lede: Free-to-play removes the purchase price entirely and earns revenue after entry, through item sales, convenience upgrades or cosmetics, with most income arriving from a small fraction of players.
body: Entry costs nothing, and the game monetises attention afterwards. Revenue arrives through a catalogue: cosmetic items, storage space, experience boosts, revival tokens, or timers that money can skip. Because a minority of players account for most spending, design optimises for population size first and conversion second, which makes onboarding, social hooks and retention systems more consequential to the business than any individual purchase in the store.

Wizet's MapleStory launched in Korea in 2003 and is the release most often cited, but the model's origins are genuinely diffuse. Korean and Chinese online games had been selling items over free access for several years, in markets where boxed retail and credit cards were both weak and internet cafés were strong. Piracy made a box price unreliable, so charging for services inside a running game was simply more collectable.

Audience size grew by orders of magnitude, and the medium reached people who would never gamble sixty units of currency on something unknown. Design consequences are structural rather than incidental, since pacing gets tuned around friction that money removes, and the same lever that respects a player's time can manufacture impatience. Regulators have since taken interest in odds disclosure, spending limits and protections for minors.
f_f2p.spread: League of Legends sold champions and skins, World of Tanks charged for premium vehicles and account time, and Fortnite Battle Royale reached an enormous audience while charging only for appearance.
f_f2p.question: Which game started the free-to-play business model?

f_cosmetic_economy.lede: Cosmetic-only monetisation restricts everything sold to appearance, keeping competitive power out of the store, so spending changes how a player looks but never how they perform.
body: Store inventory is limited to skins, colours, effects, emotes, announcer voices and similar decoration. Statistics, abilities and character access are earned in play or granted outright. Holding that line is a design commitment with real edge cases, because a skin that alters a silhouette or obscures an ability's wind-up does affect play, and studios routinely rework cosmetics that made an attack harder to read.

Riot Games ran League of Legends on this basis from 2009, in a competitive genre where selling power would have destroyed the thing it was trying to build. Free-to-play had already arrived carrying a reputation for pay-to-win economies, and a competitive scene cannot survive that suspicion. Selling identity rather than advantage was the compromise that made a zero price at the door acceptable to players who cared about fairness.

Trust turned out to be commercially valuable, and cosmetic economies now sustain some of the largest games ever made while keeping their competitive layer defensible. Costs are creative and structural. Character design bends toward what will sell as a skin, the release calendar answers to store slots, and the sums involved are large enough that fairness becomes a marketing position. Boundaries also erode quietly, through convenience items and paid progression.
f_cosmetic_economy.spread: Dota 2 sold couriers and terrain, Rocket League decorated cars without touching their physics, and Fall Guys made costumes the entire contents of its store.
f_cosmetic_economy.question: Which game made cosmetic-only monetisation the standard?

f_lootbox.lede: Randomised loot boxes sell a sealed container whose contents are drawn from a weighted table, so the purchase buys a chance at a specific item rather than the item itself.
body: A box is earned in play or bought outright, opened with a key that usually costs money, and yields items drawn against probabilities that may or may not be published. Rare tiers sit at low percentages, while duplicate protection, guaranteed thresholds and tradability vary by game. Presentation carries much of the value: opening is staged with animation and sound, and where trading exists a secondary market prices the contents.

Attribution is contested. Valve added Mann Co. crates and paid keys to Team Fortress 2 in 2010, the usual Western reference point, but Asian free-to-play games had sold randomised draws for years beforehand, MapleStory's gachapon among them, and Japanese mobile gacha was already a mature business by that date. What 2010 supplied was a large Western audience, a tradable inventory, and an observable market price for luck.

Revenue was extraordinary, and the mechanic migrated into full-priced retail games, which is where it met the public. Regulators in several countries examined whether paid random rewards constitute gambling; some restricted or banned particular implementations, others required odds disclosure, and platform holders eventually mandated it. Industry response was largely a move toward purchases with known contents, which is precisely the opening that battle passes walked through.
f_lootbox.spread: Hearthstone built card acquisition on packs, Overwatch tied boxes to progression before removing them entirely, and Genshin Impact runs published odds with a guaranteed pull threshold.
f_lootbox.question: Which game introduced loot boxes?

f_battle_pass.lede: A seasonal battle pass sells a fixed progression track for a limited period, releasing known cosmetic rewards as the buyer completes challenges and climbs tiers before the season expires.
body: Buying the pass unlocks a numbered track, often a hundred tiers deep. Playing earns points toward the next tier, while daily and weekly challenges accelerate the climb. Rewards are listed in advance and visible from the start, and a thinner free track runs in parallel for everyone else. Everything is bound to a season of fixed length, and tiers left unclaimed when the clock runs out are usually forfeited.

Valve introduced the format for Dota 2 in 2013 as a compendium attached to its annual tournament, with purchases also inflating the prize pool. Fortnite Battle Royale is what generalised it into the industry default a few years later, so credit is genuinely split between the invention and the popularisation. Motivation was partly regulatory: known contents avoid the gambling comparison that loot boxes attracted, and a schedule produces forecastable revenue.

Randomness was traded for obligation. Players know exactly what they will receive and exactly what they must do to earn it, which is fairer and also more demanding, since the reward depends on playing enough before a deadline. Designers gained a lever for steering behaviour through missions, which can distort how a game is actually played. Whether the format respects players or rents their time is argued from both directions.
f_battle_pass.spread: Fortnite Battle Royale made the seasonal track an industry default, Valorant ran parallel free and paid tiers, and Helldivers 2 sold passes that never expire.
f_battle_pass.question: Which game invented the battle pass?

f_live_service.lede: Live-service seasonal content organises a game as a calendar, with story, activities, rewards and economy arriving in scheduled seasons and frequently expiring when the next season begins.
body: Operation replaces release. Content lands on a published schedule of seasons and events, weekly resets rotate whatever is worth doing, and much of it is time-limited: a store rotation, an activity, or a storyline that closes for good when the season ends. Servers hold authoritative state so the game can be altered underneath players, and the installed client is expected to update constantly.

Bungie built Destiny in 2014 as a shooter with the operating structure of a massively multiplayer game, financed by a publishing deal that assumed years of support rather than a single sale. Persistent worlds had run seasonal events for a decade, and the season pass had already normalised selling a schedule. Combining them made the calendar itself the product, which suits both recurring revenue and a permanent development team.

Games gained lifespans measured in years and communities with a shared weekly rhythm, which genuinely serves players who want somewhere to return to. Costs are unusually visible. Expiring content cannot be preserved or played later, the schedule presses on players and staff alike, and a game that must always feel current drifts toward a treadmill. Several prominent services have closed entirely, taking everything bought inside them.
f_live_service.spread: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege reworked maps and operators each season, Pokémon GO pinned events to real-world dates, and Overwatch 2 rebuilt its economy around seasonal delivery.
f_live_service.question: What does live service mean in video games?

f_early_access.lede: Paid early access sells an unfinished game to players who fund and test it, with development continuing in public and buyers acting as audience, revenue and feedback loop simultaneously.
body: Access is sold before completion, often at a discount that rises as release approaches. Buyers receive updates as they land, sometimes weekly, and report problems directly to a small team that answers in public. Development priorities shift in response to what players actually do, and the boundary between testing and playing dissolves. Some games leave early access within a year, and some never leave it at all.

Markus Persson sold Minecraft in alpha from 2009, turning a side project into a company on the strength of something unfinished. Precedent existed in shareware, where a playable portion circulated freely and payment unlocked the rest, and crowdfunding was arriving in parallel, so the claim is shared. Cheap payment processing and digital distribution supplied the missing pieces; formal storefront support for the model followed a few years later.

Small teams gained a way to finance ambitious work without a publisher, and several of the most influential games of the past fifteen years exist only because of it. Expectation carries the cost. Players buy a promise, some projects stall or disappear, and public development pulls a design toward what the current audience wants rather than what the game needs. Reviewing a moving target is close to meaningless.
f_early_access.spread: Kerbal Space Program grew its physics in public, Baldur's Gate 3 spent years refining one act with players, and Hades tuned combat through frequent builds before its full release.
f_early_access.question: Which game started the paid early access model?

f_mobile_f2p.lede: Mobile free-to-play designs around short, interruptible sessions, using energy timers, level maps and in-app purchases to monetise a phone audience that plays in minutes rather than hours.
body: Sessions are built to run a few minutes and to end at a decision point. Attempts are rationed by an energy meter that refills in real time, so failing a level costs a life and eventually costs waiting. Purchases sell the removal of that wait, extra moves at the moment of failure, or boosts that resolve a stubborn level. A map screen tracks progress and shows where friends have reached.

King released Candy Crush Saga in 2012 across phones and a social network, refining mechanics that browser and social games had already established, energy systems and viral invitations among them. Hardware and payment infrastructure had just aligned: touchscreens everywhere, app stores holding a stored card, and a general audience that had never bought a game. Free entry was the only way to reach people who would not evaluate a price at all.

By revenue this became the dominant form of the medium, funded largely by a small share of players spending heavily. Measurement drives the design consequences, since every element is instrumented and tuned against retention and conversion, which favours legible loops and steady friction over authorial risk. Regulators have responded to spending by minors and to undisclosed odds, and several jurisdictions now require refunds, limits or disclosure.
f_mobile_f2p.spread: Clash of Clans put timers on base construction, Pokémon GO monetised movement through physical space, and Genshin Impact combined phone-length sessions with published-odds character banners.
f_mobile_f2p.question: Why do mobile games make you wait for lives?

f_los_detection.lede: Line-of-sight detection gives enemies a limited field of view, so they can fail to notice a player, and the game starts tracking what its characters know separately from what is true.
body: Each guard carries a facing and a cone or radius of vision, and detection becomes a question of geometry: where the player stands, what lies between them, whether the guard has turned. Sightlines break on walls, cover, distance and darkness. Because knowledge is held per character rather than globally, one room can contain several conflicting beliefs about it, and manipulating those beliefs is the actual gameplay.

Muse Software built Castle Wolfenstein in 1981 around guards who could be avoided rather than only fought, a pointed idea when most games modelled opponents as pursuers that always knew the player's position. Memory constraints helped, since a facing and a short check are cheap. Design intent mattered more: a game about escaping a fortress needs enemies whose attention is a resource to be managed.

An entire genre followed, along with a broader principle that combat can be a failure state rather than a goal. Legibility and fragility are the costs. Players cannot see a vision cone unless the game draws one, so detections often feel unfair, and such systems break memorably when a guard spots a body through a wall or forgets a firefight. Modern versions spend heavily on communicating what enemies perceive.
f_los_detection.spread: Metal Gear Solid formalised cones and alert states, Thief: The Dark Project added measured light and sound as inputs, and Alien: Isolation gave one unscripted hunter its own senses.
f_los_detection.question: Which game first let enemies fail to see the player?

f_alert_states.lede: Graduated alert states move enemies through named stages of awareness, from unaware to suspicious, alerted and searching and back again, so being spotted becomes recoverable rather than terminal.
body: Awareness is a state machine with timers. A noise pushes a guard into suspicion and sends them to investigate; a clear sighting triggers full alert, reinforcements and a countdown. Finding nobody drops the group into a search phase where patrols widen and behaviour stays cautious, and only after that does the level return to normal. Each stage carries its own music, animation set and rules of engagement.

Konami Computer Entertainment Japan built the system for Metal Gear Solid in 1998, when three-dimensional space made perfect avoidance unrealistic and instant failure intolerable. Earlier stealth games often restarted the level on detection, punishing experimentation exactly where it was most needed. Modelling awareness as a curve let designers keep tension alive after a mistake, and gave players something to do with that mistake besides reloading.

Stealth became a genre people finished rather than abandoned, and the vocabulary spread well beyond it into open worlds and horror. Pacing and honesty are what it costs. Waiting out a search timer inside a locker is dull, and the states feel arbitrary when a guard forgets a body or remembers one forever. Designers still argue whether a return to unaware is a mercy or a lie the fiction cannot carry.
f_alert_states.spread: Assassin's Creed drove alert through crowds and rooftops, Alien: Isolation refused to let its hunter fully forget, and The Last of Us Part II tied searching to spoken enemy coordination.
f_alert_states.question: Which game introduced alert phases in stealth games?

f_detection_meter.lede: Explicit detection feedback shows players what enemies currently perceive, using meters, icons, vision cones or sound indicators to turn a hidden system into readable and teachable information.
body: Perception is drawn on screen. Awareness may appear as a filling meter above a guard, a symbol at the moment of detection, a cone on the map showing where someone can see, or a marker for the last known position they are moving toward. Some games render noise as expanding rings. Whatever the form, the display describes the enemy's belief rather than the truth of the situation.

Konami Computer Entertainment Japan added radar and alert indicators to Metal Gear Solid in 1998 because a three-dimensional stealth game is otherwise played by guesswork. Camera limits made judging sightlines by eye unreliable, and nobody learns a system whose rules they never observe. Exposing the internal state converted a source of frustration into a tactical display, and turned difficulty into a matter of planning rather than luck.

Stealth became teachable, and skill shifted from cautious crawling toward reading and manipulating attention. Immersion pays for it. A cone drawn on a map is a chart rather than a place, and players watching the chart stop watching the world, which is why some games withhold the display or offer a mode without it. Where exactly the line falls between fairness and hand-holding remains unsettled.
f_detection_meter.spread: Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell reduced the display to light and sound meters, while Hitman: Blood Money compressed enemy awareness into a single visible suspicion bar.
f_detection_meter.question: Which game first showed players an enemy detection meter?

f_light_shadow.lede: Light-and-shadow stealth measures illumination and sound as concrete quantities, so standing in darkness or moving across soft ground genuinely changes whether guards can perceive the player.
body: Brightness at the player's position is sampled and reported, often through a visible gem or meter, and guards test against that value rather than against a scripted trigger. Sound behaves the same way: footsteps carry differently on stone, wood, carpet and water, and slowing down quietens them. Water arrows extinguish torches and moss arrows lay quiet ground, so lighting and materials become a system the player edits.

Looking Glass Studios shipped Thief: The Dark Project in 1998, having built a first-person game around avoidance at a moment when the perspective meant shooting. Their engine could report light values and surface materials cheaply, which made those properties usable as rules rather than decoration. Design followed the technology: if darkness can be measured, a level can be composed in light the way another game composes cover.

Lighting stopped being art direction and became level design, a shift visible in every stealth game since and in how immersive sims treat environments as systems. Graphics brought the costs. Modern dynamic lighting makes a stable, readable darkness value hard to guarantee, and players resent being spotted in a shadow that looked solid. Several later games abandoned measured light for scripted visibility simply because it is easier to tune.
f_light_shadow.spread: Thief II: The Metal Age refined the same rules, Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell built levels around shootable lights, and Amnesia: The Dark Descent made hiding in darkness dangerous in itself.
f_light_shadow.question: Which game made light and shadow a stealth mechanic?

f_immersive_sim.lede: Systemic solution spaces build a game from consistent interacting rules rather than authored answers, so problems can be solved in ways the designers never anticipated and never wrote down.
body: Rules are general rather than local. Objects have physical properties, characters have senses and allegiances, fire spreads, water conducts, and a key is one option among several. Because those rules apply everywhere instead of only where a designer expected them, a locked door might be opened, bypassed through a window, avoided entirely, or made irrelevant by persuading someone else to open it. Designers author obstacles; solutions emerge.

Blue Sky Productions built Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss in 1992 as a first-person role-playing game with real geometry, physical objects and characters who could be talked to rather than only fought. Ambition rather than constraint drove the work, and the studio's later projects carried the approach forward. Its founding promise is a contract: if something looks like it should work, the simulation ought to honour the attempt.

Games built this way produce a strong sense of ownership, because a solution the player invented feels like theirs, and they support replaying in ways linear designs cannot. Severe costs explain the small output. Interacting systems generate bugs and unwinnable states, testing is combinatorial, and much of what gets built is never seen by any one player. Commercial results have been inconsistent enough that studios keep abandoning the form.
f_immersive_sim.spread: Deus Ex extended the contract to conversation and level routing, Thief: The Dark Project narrowed it to stealth, and Prey pushed material transformation to its logical extreme.
f_immersive_sim.question: What was the first immersive sim?

f_social_stealth.lede: Social stealth hides the player through behaviour rather than geometry, using crowds, disguises and unremarkable conduct to pass unnoticed in open daylight instead of in shadow.
body: Concealment depends on conduct. Walking at a normal pace, blending into a group, sitting on a bench or matching the crowd's movement keeps suspicion low, while running, climbing, shoving or drawing a weapon raises it. Guards evaluate behaviour in context, so an action that is unremarkable in a market square is alarming in a restricted courtyard. Visibility is never the variable being managed here.

Ubisoft Montreal built Assassin's Creed in 2007 around crowds that new hardware could finally render in numbers, and a game about assassination in a historical city needs concealment that works at noon. Shadow-based stealth had no answer for an open street. Turning the crowd from scenery into cover solved a technical showcase and a design problem at once, since the same simulated pedestrians served both jobs.

Stealth moved into daylight, bringing a different fantasy with it: not the intruder in the dark but the person nobody looks at twice. Subtlety and consistency are the costs. Crowd rules are hard to communicate, so players often cannot tell why they were noticed, and a system that reduces blending to standing near four people becomes a ritual rather than tension. Later entries mixed social and shadow approaches instead of choosing.
f_social_stealth.spread: Assassin's Creed II gave blending dedicated crowd behaviours and hiding spots, and Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag adapted the same rules to crowded port towns and taverns.
f_social_stealth.question: Which game let you hide in a crowd instead of the shadows?

f_3d_audio_stealth.lede: Diegetic three-dimensional audio carries real tactical information, using footstep material, distance, direction and occlusion so that a player can locate and identify threats by listening alone.
body: Sound is simulated rather than decorated. Footsteps differ by surface, so a guard on stone is audible much further than one on carpet; volume falls with distance, walls muffle and redirect, and positional mixing lets a player place a source behind a door. Guards make noise deliberately, muttering and jangling, while players make it accidentally, so listening and staying quiet are two halves of one skill.

Looking Glass Studios built Thief: The Dark Project in 1998 around a first-person game in which the player mostly avoids what they can hear, and invested in an audio system able to report material, distance and occlusion. Consumer sound hardware had just made positional mixing practical. Necessity shaped it further, because a game played in darkness cannot rely on the eyes to carry threat information.

Ears became a primary sensor, and the technique carried into horror, competitive shooters and survival games, where footstep audio is now a core skill. Equipment and access are the costs. Positional information assumes headphones and unimpaired hearing, so games leaning on it exclude players unless visual indicators are added, which is now common practice. Speaker layouts, streaming compression and mixing choices all degrade the signal further.
f_3d_audio_stealth.spread: Alien: Isolation used sound to track an unscripted hunter, Phasmophobia built its investigation on careful listening, and Lethal Company turned proximity audio into information and comedy at once.
f_3d_audio_stealth.question: Which game made sound a stealth mechanic?

f_level_editor.lede: A bundled level editor ships the authoring tool inside the game itself, letting players build, save and share their own levels from exactly the pieces the original designer used.
body: Tools sit in the menu beside the campaign. Players place platforms, enemies, items and exits on the same grid the shipped levels use, test immediately, and save the result. Because the editor writes the format the game reads, a player-made level is indistinguishable from an official one, and distribution becomes a matter of passing a file to somebody else by whatever means exist.

Douglas E. Smith included an editor with Lode Runner in 1983, when a level was a grid layout and the tool that produced the shipped levels had already been written. Home computers arrived with an expectation that owners would type and create rather than only consume. Shipping the editor therefore cost very little and converted a fixed set of a hundred and fifty levels into an open-ended one.

Players became designers without asking permission, and the pipeline from making levels to making games has run through this door ever since. Quality control and support are the costs, since most user levels are poor and the good ones need to be findable, which is why later systems added ratings and curation. Editors also constrain, because a level built from a game's pieces can only argue within them.
f_level_editor.spread: Duke Nukem 3D shipped its build tool, Unreal Tournament included the editor used to make it, and Super Smash Bros. Brawl let players assemble stages from parts and trade them.
f_level_editor.question: Which game first shipped with a level editor?

f_mod_sdk.lede: Open data formats and modding kits let players replace a game's levels, art and rules without its source code, treating the engine as a platform and the content as swappable files.
body: Assets live in archives the game reads at runtime, so replacing an archive replaces the content: maps, textures, sounds, weapons, enemy behaviour. Documentation, or a community's reverse engineering of the format, lets outsiders write tools against it. Later engines formalise the arrangement with scripting languages and published development kits, and total conversions built this way can share nothing with the original except the executable.

id Software separated Doom's engine from its data in 1993 and, unusually for the period, took an encouraging position toward the editors that appeared within weeks; a source release followed later. Self-interest played a part, because a game people keep making things for keeps selling. Culture mattered as much, given founders who had come up modifying other people's software on shared machines.

Free apprenticeship at scale is the consequence. Whole genres arrived as mods before they arrived as products, and a generation of studios was staffed by people whose first work was unpaid content for someone else's engine. Ownership and labour are the costs. Value created by that work accrues mostly to the platform holder, moddable games carry support and cheating burdens, and studios often close the door once a title becomes commercially sensitive.
f_mod_sdk.spread: Half-Life produced Counter-Strike, Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos hosted Defense of the Ancients, and The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim sustained a modding scene larger than most development teams.
f_mod_sdk.question: Which game started modding culture?

f_ugc_marketplace.lede: A user-content marketplace lets players build, publish and sell inside the platform itself, with the operator providing hosting, discovery and payment while taking a share of every transaction.
body: Creation, distribution and payment sit in one place. Players build with the platform's tools, publish straight to an audience already present, and sell access or items priced in a platform currency that converts back into money above a threshold. Operators take a cut, control discovery and recommendation, and set the rules for what may be sold, which makes them landlord, bank and censor simultaneously.

Roblox Corporation launched in 2006 with creation as the product rather than a feature, and grew for years on an audience of young builders before its payout system matured. Precedent came from mod communities, which had already proved that players will make and share content but had no way to pay anyone. Adding a currency and a conversion path turned a hobby into an economy with real, if very uneven, incomes.

Supply became effectively unlimited, and a catalogue grew faster than any studio could author. Labour and governance carry the consequences. Revenue splits favour the operator heavily, many creators are minors, and moderating a live economy full of user content is unsolved at scale. Regulators and journalists have examined both pay rates and child safety, so the platform model itself is now the thing under scrutiny.
f_ugc_marketplace.spread: LittleBigPlanet published player levels into a curated feed, and Cities: Skylines routed community assets and mods through a storefront that made them installable in one click.
f_ugc_marketplace.question: Which game let players sell what they made inside it?

f_ingame_creation.lede: In-game creation suites place the authoring tools inside the game world itself, so players build levels and objects with a controller while standing in the space they are making.
body: Editing happens in the same space as playing. A character or cursor manipulates physical objects directly, dragging out material, attaching bolts and switches, wiring logic between parts, then switching to play and testing on the spot. Tools are taught through the campaign rather than a manual, and every asset used by the shipped levels is available. Publishing and browsing are built in, so sharing never leaves the game.

Media Molecule released LittleBigPlanet in 2008 on a console with no keyboard, which ruled out a conventional editor from the start. Their answer was to make authoring a physical activity performed with the same controls used to play, taught the way the game teaches everything else. Commercially the point was a product that keeps producing content indefinitely without the studio having to build any of it.

Creation as play brought in people who would never open a level editor, particularly younger players, and produced enormous volumes of levels. Ceilings are the cost. Controller-driven tools are slower and less precise than a mouse, complex logic becomes physically laborious, and once millions of levels exist discovery matters more than authoring. Servers eventually close, which erases most of what was made.
f_ingame_creation.spread: Halo: Reach turned map editing into an in-match toolset, and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom let players bolt vehicles together from scattered parts.
f_ingame_creation.question: Which game let you build levels with a controller?

f_replay_share.lede: Replay capture records a match as game data rather than video, letting players rewatch it from any camera angle, pause anywhere, and export screenshots or clips to share.
body: Rather than storing pixels, the game stores inputs and events and re-simulates the match during playback. Because the world is rebuilt instead of replayed, the camera comes free: it can detach from any player, fly, slow down, or sit inside an explosion. Files are tiny next to video. Screenshots and short clips can be pulled from any moment and uploaded to a service outside the game entirely.

Bungie added saved films and a theatre mode to Halo 3 in 2007, alongside a web service that hosted whatever players captured. Determinism in the engine made it feasible, since a match already had to be reconstructible from inputs for networking reasons. Cultural timing supplied the rest, arriving as video sharing sites became mainstream while capture hardware was still expensive and awkward for console players.

Play turned into media, and the clip economy that now drives discovery for competitive games grew straight out of this capability. Consequences include a quiet change in how people play, because a highlight worth clipping is not always the correct decision. Fragility is the technical cost: a replay depends on the exact build that produced it, so patches invalidate archives and long-term preservation is close to impossible.
f_replay_share.spread: Super Meat Boy replayed every failed attempt at once as a crowd of runners, and Rocket League built a replay viewer that competitive players and broadcasters use to review positioning.
f_replay_share.question: Which game introduced saved match replays and sharing?

f_rts_base.lede: Real-time base building has players harvest resources, raise production buildings and field armies under continuous time pressure, with no turns and every task competing for the same attention.
body: One loop drives everything: gather a resource, spend it on buildings, buildings produce units, units take ground and protect the harvesters. Time never stops, so construction and combat compete for attention and for the same income. Units are selected with a mouse and ordered directly, production queues run in the background, and a technology tree gates stronger options behind earlier buildings.

Westwood Studios assembled the template in Dune II in 1992, drawing on earlier real-time experiments and on the mouse-driven interface home computers had recently standardised. Its licence supplied a setting where resource harvesting was already the fiction. Consolidation rather than invention was the achievement: sidebar production, direct unit selection, a harvest economy and a technology tree arranged into a shape that finally worked.

Nearly every strategy game since has argued with that arrangement, by extending it, stripping the base out, or collapsing the whole thing onto a single unit. Costs are baked into the format. Real-time play rewards mechanical speed as much as judgement, the opening minutes are usually a memorised routine, and a match can be decided by an economic lead long before anything visible happens.
f_rts_base.spread: Command & Conquer added filmed briefings and faction asymmetry, StarCraft balanced three genuinely different economies, and Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings stretched the loop across historical ages.
f_rts_base.question: Which game created the real-time strategy formula?

f_turn_grid_tactics.lede: Turn-based grid tactics play out on squares, each side moving a roster of individual units in sequence, with those units carrying experience, equipment and consequences from battle to battle.
body: Movement is counted in tiles and bounded by terrain cost. Units alternate by side, attack from adjacent or ranged positions, and take advantages from height, cover, facing or weapon type. Persistence is what separates the form from a board game: characters level up, learn skills, form relationships and, in some designs, die permanently, so a decision made on one battlefield echoes through the remainder of the campaign.

Intelligent Systems released Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light in 1990 on hardware that suited the form exactly. A grid is cheap to draw, turns need no processing headroom, and a console audience could take as long as it liked over a move. Combining wargame structure with role-playing progression gave individual soldiers names and histories, which is precisely what makes losing one land.

Two decades of tactical role-playing games follow from that merger, and the format survives because it scales down to modest hardware and up to considerable depth. Pace and punishment are the costs. Battles run long, one mistake can be irreversible where death is permanent, and reloading becomes the rational response, which many designs then legislate against with checkpoints or forgiving modes.
f_turn_grid_tactics.spread: X-COM: UFO Defense added fog of war and hidden movement, Final Fantasy Tactics layered job classes onto the grid, and Into the Breach showed every enemy action one turn ahead.
f_turn_grid_tactics.question: Which game created the tactical grid RPG?

f_4x_empire.lede: Turn-based 4X games ask players to explore, expand, exploit and exterminate across a map and a timeline, growing a civilisation from one settler into an empire over hundreds of turns.
body: Play spans scales that other genres keep separate. Cities are founded and specialised, terrain is improved, research advances a technology tree, diplomacy and war run alongside trade, and a single turn may cover a decade. Victory conditions are plural, including conquest, science and culture, so one map supports incompatible strategies. Decisions compound slowly, which makes an early choice about where to settle unusually heavy.

Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley built Sid Meier's Civilization at MicroProse in 1991, drawing on board wargames, city-building software and earlier historical simulations. Turn-based structure was partly a practical necessity, since simulating a world in real time was out of reach, but it also matched the subject. History is a sequence of decisions with long consequences, and a turn is a reasonable unit for one of them.

History became something a player argues with rather than reads, and the genre's grip is famous enough to have generated its own vocabulary about lost evenings. Consequences are political too, because any model of civilisation encodes claims about progress, colonisation and violence that later designers have revisited deliberately. Late-game tedium remains the persistent design problem, since a won game still demands hours of administration.
f_4x_empire.spread: Master of Orion moved the formula into space, Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri gave its factions ideologies, and Europa Universalis traded the technology ladder for continuous historical simulation.
f_4x_empire.question: Which game invented the 4X strategy genre?

f_tower_defense.lede: Tower defense has players place static defences along a fixed route while waves of enemies walk it, turning strategy into a problem of positioning, coverage and upgrade timing.
body: Attackers follow a path and rarely fight back directly, while defenders are immobile and pay for range, damage type and rate of fire. Resources come from kills, so each wave funds preparation for the next. Difficulty climbs through waves with different resistances and speeds, and the real decisions concern where to spend, when to upgrade rather than expand, and how far placement can lengthen the route.

Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos supplied the tools in 2003, and the genre grew inside its custom map scene rather than being designed as a product; Blizzard Entertainment built the editor and players built the form. Older ancestors are frequently cited, including arcade games about defending a position and comparable maps in earlier strategy titles. Free tools plus an audience of map makers turned an idea into a category.

Spinning out of a mod scene into standalone games happened quickly, and the format suited browsers and phones unusually well because it needs no reflexes and pauses gracefully. Depth and repetition are the costs. Optimal layouts exist and can be looked up, which reduces strategy to executing a known answer, so later designs add randomised waves, restricted placement or hero units to keep decisions live.
f_tower_defense.spread: Clash Royale rebuilt lane denial as a two-player card duel on a phone, keeping the towers and the pathing while replacing static defences with timed unit deployment.
f_tower_defense.question: Where did tower defense games come from?

f_deck_progression.lede: Deck-building run progression makes the deck itself the character, assembled from cards offered during a single run and then discarded completely when that run comes to an end.
body: A run opens with a weak starting deck and a branching map. Each fight offers a card as a reward, shops sell more, and relics rewrite rules for the rest of the attempt. Adding cards dilutes the deck, so refusing a reward is a genuine move and card removal is a service worth paying for. Death resets everything except unlocks, which widen future options rather than strengthen the next attempt.

Mega Crit released Slay the Spire into early access in 2017, joining two forms that had matured separately: the tabletop deck-builder, where a deck is constructed during play rather than before it, and the roguelike run with procedural layout and permadeath. Both are built from randomised, self-contained decisions. Merging them swapped the roguelike's item build for a deck, which is legible, tunable and cheap to author.

Imitators arrived by the dozen, and card-based runs became a default structure for small teams because content scales through combination rather than through art. Costs are the familiar ones for randomised design. A run can be lost to a bad offer rather than a bad decision, and the probability reading that experts do fluently is opaque to newcomers. Balance work is effectively endless.
f_deck_progression.spread: Balatro applied the same run structure to poker hands, letting jokers rewrite scoring in place of card rewards while an escalating ante replaced the branching map.
f_deck_progression.question: Which game combined deck-building with roguelike runs?

f_dynamic_music.lede: Adaptive dynamic music follows the player, transitioning between arrangements on musical boundaries so a score can change with the scene without cutting off or restarting a track.
body: Music is stored as sequences with marked branch points rather than as a finished recording. When the game state changes, the system waits for the next musically sensible moment, then moves to a matching arrangement, adding instruments, shifting key, or crossing into a variation. Because transitions land on the beat, the score sounds composed rather than switched, and a theme can follow a character from room to room.

Lucasfilm Games shipped Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge in 1991 with an interactive music system built by the studio's own composers for exactly this problem. Adventure games created the need, since a player may stand in one room for a minute or twenty and the music has to survive both. Sequenced formats made it possible, because a score held as instructions can be rearranged in ways a recording cannot.

Scores stopped looping and started responding, which is now standard practice and has produced its own compositional discipline of layers, stems and vertical arrangement. Authorship pays for it. Music written to recombine must work in many orders, which limits long-form development, and a dynamic system can smear a strong cue into wallpaper. Composers still argue about how much control to hand over to a state machine.
f_dynamic_music.spread: Star Wars: TIE Fighter scored dogfights with the same system, Grand Theft Auto III made its music diegetic radio, and Journey layered a score around wordless multiplayer encounters.
f_dynamic_music.question: Which game first used music that changes with what the player does?

f_beat_match.lede: Beat-matched input judges the player against a musical grid, scoring each press by how closely it lands on the beat rather than by whether the right button was chosen.
body: Timing carries the entire judgement. Prompts appear in a pattern tied to the music, and a press is graded by its distance from the target moment, usually into a few named bands running from perfect down to miss. Performance then feeds back into the audio: a poor run degrades the track or the vocalist, a good one embellishes it, so the score and the scoring are one object.

NanaOn-Sha released PaRappa the Rapper in 1996 on a console with a disc drive, which finally made streamed music of decent quality practical. Masaya Matsuura came from music rather than games, and the design treats call-and-response rap as the interaction itself: the game performs a phrase, the player repeats it. Rhythm-scored play existed earlier in Japan, but this is the release that established the form commercially.

Time became the difficulty axis, which is unusually accessible, because the rules are audible and anyone who can nod along already understands the system. Latency and licensing are the costs. Audio and display delay must be measured and compensated or the game is simply unfair, and music rights make the genre expensive while quietly removing old titles from sale. Precision requirements also exclude some disabled players.
f_beat_match.spread: Dance Dance Revolution moved judgement to the feet, Guitar Hero attached it to a plastic instrument, and Beat Saber rebuilt the same timing windows around motion controllers in virtual reality.
f_beat_match.question: Which game invented the rhythm game?

f_note_highway.lede: A scrolling note highway renders upcoming inputs as objects travelling toward a fixed judgement line, turning a musical part into something a stranger can sight-read within seconds.
body: Notes approach along lanes at a speed tied to the tempo, and each lane maps to one control. Hitting a note as it reaches the line scores it, sustained notes are held, and chords arrive as simultaneous rows. Because the display shows the future, the interface teaches continuously: a player reads density and spacing well ahead of time and prepares, rather than reacting to a cue at the moment it lands.

Konami introduced the arrangement with GuitarFreaks in 1998 in arcades, where a machine has seconds to explain itself to somebody standing in front of it holding money. Traditional notation is unreadable at that speed by that audience. Mapping pitch to lanes and time to distance removed any need for musical literacy, and the vertical layout also survives being watched over a player's shoulder by a crowd.

Something genuinely universal came out of it, and the same layout now appears across instruments, dance mats, touchscreens and virtual reality. Trade-offs are musical. Lanes flatten harmony into a handful of positions, so the display teaches pattern recognition more than music, and charting is an authored discipline of wildly varying quality. Scroll speed and readability are accessibility issues that many implementations still ignore.
f_note_highway.spread: Dance Dance Revolution ran arrows upward to a fixed line, Guitar Hero angled the lanes into a receding fretboard, and Beat Saber replaced it with blocks approaching in three dimensions.
f_note_highway.question: Which game invented the scrolling note chart in rhythm games?

f_peripheral_instrument.lede: Instrument peripherals replace the controller with a physical object shaped like the thing being played, so posture, grip and gesture carry the fantasy as much as the timing does.
body: Hardware carries the design. A guitar-shaped controller has coloured fret buttons, a strum bar and a whammy, requiring both hands to do different jobs in coordination, and tilting it upward triggers a bonus. Because the object resembles an instrument, holding it properly becomes part of the performance and onlookers can read what a player is doing. Charting must then make five plastic buttons feel like the recording.

Harmonix released Guitar Hero in 2005 with a guitar controller in the box, though Konami's arcade machines had used guitar-shaped inputs since 1998, so the hardware idea was not new and the credit is properly shared. Context is what changed: a console peripheral aimed at Western living rooms, priced for a household, packaged with familiar rock music. Bundling hardware with software also produced margins that pure software lacked.

Living rooms filled with plastic instruments, and a large non-gaming audience arrived with them, briefly making music games one of the industry's largest categories. Collapse was structural rather than a matter of taste. Peripherals are expensive, bulky, single-purpose and incompatible between titles, retailers withdrew the shelf space, and annual releases exhausted the audience. Later music games mostly returned to standard controllers or hardware people already owned.
f_peripheral_instrument.spread: Guitar Hero III: Legends of Rock pushed the guitar toward a competitive standard, Rock Band added drums and vocals for a full band, and DJ Hero shipped a turntable controller.
f_peripheral_instrument.question: Which game started the plastic guitar controller craze?

f_rhythm_combat.lede: Rhythm-locked action requires every move and attack to land on the beat, fusing a music game's timing discipline with the tactical decisions of a dungeon crawl.
body: Movement, attacks and item use each cost one beat, and missing the beat costs a turn or a scoring multiplier. Enemies act on their own rhythmic patterns, so a skeleton that moves every second beat is a timing puzzle as much as a threat. Because the music sets the clock, tempo becomes difficulty, and a faster track compresses the time available to decide where to step next.

Brace Yourself Games released Crypt of the NecroDancer in 2015, joining two genres that solve each other's pacing problems. Turn-based roguelikes let players deliberate indefinitely, which drains tension, while rhythm games have relentless pace and nothing to decide. Locking turns to a beat imposes a clock on the first and gives the second something to think about, and procedurally built floors keep those choices fresh across attempts.

Tension of a specific kind results, since planning happens while a metronome runs, and music stops being accompaniment and becomes the rule set. Reach is limited. Demanding rhythm and tactics together excludes people competent at only one, and the difficulty cannot be softened much without breaking the premise, which is why implementations tend to offer a beat-free mode as an accommodation rather than as a variant.
f_rhythm_combat.spread: Adoption stayed narrow, with no tracked title inheriting the beat-locked turn wholesale; later designers tend to borrow the idea for single encounters rather than as a game's base rule.
f_rhythm_combat.question: Which game combined a rhythm game with a roguelike?
